Officious

uh-FISH-us · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Officious is aggressively offering unwanted advice or help, pressing in where no one has asked for it.

An officious neighbor kept knocking to tell the new family exactly how they should mow their own lawn.

Worked Example

The officious new intern kept rearranging coworkers' desks and correcting their emails without anyone asking for his help.

Rearranging desks and correcting emails no one asked about is exactly officious meddling.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

meddlesome: Meddlesome means interfering in other people's affairs -- prying, snooping, poking into business that is not yours. Officious is more specific: the interference comes dressed as help, aggressively offering advice or assistance nobody asked for. A meddlesome person pries; an officious one insists on 'helping.'

intrusive: Intrusive describes anything that forces its way in where it is not wanted -- a noise, a question, a camera at the window. Officious is narrower: a person pushily offering unwanted help or advice. An intrusion can be silent; officious conduct always arrives with 'assistance.'

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

deferential: respectfully yielding to others

Where it sits · how hard they push into your affairs — bossy → officious → overbearing

bossy vs. officious: Bossy is a casual, everyday word for someone who likes giving orders; officious adds a specific, meddling eagerness to offer help or advice that wasn't requested.

overbearing vs. officious: Overbearing implies a forceful, domineering pressure over others' decisions, while officious is about excessive, unwanted helpfulness rather than raw dominance.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — offic

root — offic: duty, service (Latin (officium))

suffix — -ious

suffix — -ious: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Officious comes from Latin officium ('duty, service') + -ious -- originally meaning simply 'dutiful,' before its meaning narrowed to describe someone who overdoes helpfulness.

Use the root in a new word: office

Use the root in a new word: office: The same officium root gives us the everyday word office -- a place of duty or service. Officious and official actually share this exact same root, even though their modern meanings have drifted apart: official describes something formally authorized, while officious describes unwanted meddling dressed up as helpfulness.
